awd_titl_txt: I-Corps: Translation Potential of Compostable Core-Shell Impact Modifiers
awd_abstract_narration:
This I-Corps project is based on the development of key additives that are compostable and turn brittle, plant-based plastics into durable materials suitable for everyday products. Currently, unmodified bioplastics like polylactic acid (PLA) break on impact, limiting use despite global demand for sustainable packaging. Each year, more than one million tons of PLA are produced, however, to improve impact strength, it must be blended with petroleum-derived additives, which negates compostability. This technology addresses the challenge by raising PLA’s impact strength by an order of magnitude while maintaining industrial compostable certification. Also, the additive may be supplied as pellets, allowing compounders, film converters, and molders to create tough, monolayer parts without changing equipment. The technology uses glycerol, which is a low-cost by-product of U.S. biodiesel, as its sole feedstock, so it may potentially displace non-degradable modifiers, streamline manufacturing, and enable new markets for bioplastics.

This I-Corps project utilizes experiential learning coupled with a first-hand investigation of the industry ecosystem to assess the translation potential of compostable core-shell particles (CCSPs) as biodegradable impact modifiers for polymer composites. The technology focuses on scalable monomer synthesis, polymerization, and integration of CCSPs into high-dosage master batches, ensuring compatibility with existing processing techniques like extrusion and compounding. The CCSPs are synthesized from glycerol-ketal acrylate monomers and the technology employs seed-fed semi-batch emulsion polymerization to produce 200–350 nm particles with an ester cross-linked rubbery core and an acrylic shell that bonds seamlessly with the bioplastic matrix. At modest loading, CCSP-modified PLA exceeds 200 J m⁻¹ Izod impact strength, which is ten times unmodified PLA strength, without sacrificing compostability. Hydrolysis studies show 90% mass loss within ten weeks under accelerated compost conditions, confirming rapid end-of-life degradation. The technology addresses key limitations of bioplastics: brittleness and limited durability. Compostable CCSPs may offer a sustainable alternative to conventional impact modifiers, enabling industries to enhance the mechanical properties of biodegradable plastics without compromising environmental responsibility.

por.por_cntn:
This Iowa State University I-Corps project looked at how a material developed at the university could be used in commercial products. The technology uses small polymer particles to make polylactic acid (PLA) less brittle. PLA is a plastic made from renewable resources. The project focused on learning about customer needs and exploring a business model for impact modifiers that keep compostability, instead of assuming that good lab results mean there is market demand.

We used customer discovery and entrepreneurial training to explore possible uses, buying requirements, and ways to manufacture the product. The team finished the I-Corps program in December 2025 and created eight weekly business-model canvases. These documents linked our ideas about customers and products to what we learned in interviews, and we updated them as we went. At the end, we gave a final presentation that shared our lessons and suggested next steps.

The work showed that even a promising technical idea can be hard for a new supplier to bring to market. Customers vary in how fast they can try a new material, how much they need to test it, and what technical help they want. Manufacturing scale and qualification needs were just as important as the material’s features. Talking with potential customers and manufacturers helped the team think about these real-world limits when choosing a first market.

In the later weeks of the program, the business model focused on 3D-printer manufacturers and hobbyists. The team aimed to offer more durable PLA-based printed parts and formulas made for users’ needs. They looked at filament as the first product, along with support for using it and possible partnerships for distribution and manufacturing. These were ideas to test in the market, not claims that the product was finished or that sales had happened.

The project’s main contribution was linking a polymer technology to real evidence of how it could be used and adopted. More broadly, the team gained hands-on experience in questioning assumptions, understanding customer feedback, and making better decisions about commercialization. The records from discovery and the business models gave a foundation for future work without sharing private customer details.

When the program ended, the team planned to keep developing the technology through step-by-step trials with a manufacturing partner, more research and testing, and by seeking more support. Stronger biobased materials could help renewable plastics be used in more ways, but more testing is needed to prove how they perform in the market and their environmental benefits. The award helped set a clearer path for this work. More effort is still needed to qualify products, encourage commercial use, and show environmental results.
